topics.title: The Air Show Loop That Started Too Low

demand.family: It went wrong (rides, stunts, amateur engineering)

topics.hook: On 22 August 2015, a 1955 jet fighter began a loop over Shoreham and never had the height to finish it.
cause_chain: A vintage Hawker Hunter starts a display loop lower than the pilot's authorised minimum for aerobatics
It enters slower than the pilot's stated minimum and without full thrust
It reaches the top of the loop below the height needed to complete it
No escape manoeuvre is flown; the jet comes down on the busy A27 Shoreham bypass
topics.rule_after: AAIB AAR 1/2017 made 11 safety recommendations (after 7 in SB 4/2015 and 14 in SB 1/2016); the CAA tightened UK display rules: pilot display authorisations, risk assessments, and display lines kept away from crowds and roads.
topics.human_moment: Two young Worthing United footballers were driving to a match on the A27 when the jet came down.

topics.title: The Racing Plane Modified Past Its Limits

demand.family: It went wrong (rides, stunts, amateur engineering)

topics.hook: At 512 miles an hour, a 1940s fighter rebuilt for racing pitched straight up over the Reno grandstand.
cause_chain: A P-51D Mustang is heavily modified for unlimited-class racing; the changes were never flight-tested or engineered for race speed
Worn lock nuts let the elevator trim tab attachment screws loosen; one tab has a fatigue crack
The reduced stiffness lets aerodynamic flutter start at about 445 knots on lap three
The tab fails, the aircraft rolls and pitches up at 17.3 g, the pilot is incapacitated, and it dives into the box seats
topics.rule_after: NTSB AAB-12/01 (Aug 2012) and 10 recommendations (Apr 2012): engineering evaluation of racer modifications, pre-race inspections, G-awareness for pilots, and race course and crowd lines moved further from spectators.
topics.human_moment: The pilot, Jimmy Leeward, was 74 and a veteran Reno racer.

topics.title: The Drain That Was Never Built to Its Drawing
topics.hook: At 09:37 on 12 August 2020, a train on a Scottish curve met gravel that should have stayed in a drain.
cause_chain: A drain is installed on the slope above the line at Carmont in 2011-12, but not built to its design
Part of it is missing from Network Rail's drain maintenance list, so it is never inspected
Extreme rain washes debris from the drain and the ground around it onto the track
The train, at 73 mph, hits the debris and derails off a bridge
topics.rule_after: RAIB 02/2022: Network Rail overhauled extreme-weather operations (speed restrictions on weather alerts), drainage asset records and construction checks; RAIB issued its weather Summary of Learning.
topics.human_moment: The train had been turned back because a landslip blocked the line ahead; it was returning to Aberdeen when it met the debris.

topics.hook: Shortly before 1 a.m., a train nobody was driving reached 65 miles an hour as it came into Lac-Mégantic.
cause_chain: A one-person crew parks a crude-oil train on a downhill main line and sets too few hand brakes

topics.title: The Text Message That Ran a Red Signal
topics.hook: Forty-seven seconds out of Chatsworth station, the engineer's phone buzzed.
cause_chain: A Metrolink commuter train leaves Chatsworth on a single-track section shared with freight

topics.title: The Mid-Air Crash That Created the FAA

demand.family: Air crash, minute by minute, ending on the rule

topics.hook: Two airliners left Los Angeles minutes apart. Over the Grand Canyon they were at the same height.
cause_chain: TWA 2 and United 718 depart Los Angeles minutes apart, both bound east
TWA asks for a higher altitude and ends up at 21,000 ft, United's altitude
Outside controlled airspace, controllers cannot separate them; pilots must 'see and be seen'
Both weave around towering clouds over the canyon and converge
topics.rule_after: The Federal Aviation Act of 1958 (signed 23 Aug 1958) created the Federal Aviation Agency with one national air traffic control system; radar and positive control of high-altitude airspace followed.
topics.human_moment: United 718's last radio call, garbled, was later deciphered as the crew saying they were going in.

topics.title: Why Airline Pilots Now Need 1,500 Hours

demand.family: Air crash, minute by minute, ending on the rule

topics.hook: The stick shaker fired on the approach to Buffalo. The captain pulled back.
cause_chain: A regional Q400 approaches Buffalo at night in icing; the crew chats through the approach
Airspeed decays unnoticed; the stick shaker warns of a stall
The captain pulls back instead of pushing forward; the aircraft stalls and rolls

topics.human_moment: The victims' families lobbied Congress for more than a year until the law passed.

topics.title: One Phone Call Doubled the Load on This Walkway

demand.family: Bridge, dam or building: every corner cut

topics.hook: Hundreds were dancing in the hotel atrium. Above them hung two walkways on thin steel rods.
cause_chain: The original design hangs the 4th- and 2nd-floor walkways from one continuous rod per hanger
Even that connection reaches only about 60% of what the building code expected
During construction the fabricator asks, by phone, to switch to two offset rods; the change goes through without full checks
The 4th-floor box beams now carry both walkways, roughly double the load; during a tea dance the connections pull through
topics.rule_after: NBS BSS 143 (1982); the engineers lost their licences, and the profession made the structural engineer of record responsible for connection design and shop-drawing review.
topics.human_moment: Rescuers worked through the night to free people trapped under the fallen walkways.

topics.title: America's Tallest Dam and the Crack Under Its Spillway

demand.family: Bridge, dam or building: every corner cut

topics.hook: Water had been getting under the concrete for decades. In February 2017 the chute broke open.

topics.title: One Unit Mistake Lost a $125M Spacecraft
topics.hook: After nine months on the way to Mars, the spacecraft arrived far lower than planned.
cause_chain: Lockheed Martin's ground software ('Small Forces') reports thruster impulse in pound-force seconds
JPL's navigation software reads the numbers as newton-seconds, about 4.45 times smaller
Every small thruster firing is under-counted; the trajectory error grows for months
Doubts are raised informally but not escalated; the orbiter arrives too low and is lost
topics.rule_after: NASA Mishap Investigation Board (Phase I, 10 Nov 1999): end-to-end verification of software interfaces and units, and a formal path for engineers to escalate concerns.
topics.human_moment: Navigators had noticed the trajectory didn't fit, and said so, but the worry never stopped the mission.

topics.title: The Ferry That Sailed With Its Doors Open
topics.hook: The bow doors were open. Nobody on the bridge could see them, and nobody had to report it.
cause_chain: The assistant bosun, whose job is to close the bow doors, is asleep when the ferry leaves Zeebrugge

topics.title: The Refinery Tower They Overfilled
topics.hook: The gauge said the tower's level was fine. It was filling to the top.
cause_chain: During start-up, operators fill the raffinate splitter tower far above its normal level; the level reading is wrong

topics.title: A tanker's rudder jammed on the Mississippi; two minutes later it hit a docked riverboat, which capsized in 22 minutes (NTSB, preliminary)

demand.title: What REALLY Happened in the New Orleans Ship Collision?

topics.hook: On the thirteenth of November, a 520-foot tanker on the Mississippi lost its steering. It had two minutes.
cause_chain: The Atlantic Asphalt's steering fails and holds its rudder hard to starboard (NTSB, preliminary)
The tanker swings toward the east bank where the riverboat American Heritage is docked at mile 96
The data recorder logs anchor and emergency ship-handling orders; two minutes after the rudder stuck, it hits
The riverboat rolls onto its side in about 22 minutes; all 190 aboard are accounted for
topics.rule_after: None yet: the NTSB will publish a preliminary report and later a probable cause; the Coast Guard classed it a major marine casualty. End on what investigators will check and when.

topics.title: FedEx Flight 80: an MD-11 bounced three times at Narita and its wing broke off on the third touchdown

demand.title: Its Just a Normal RC Airplane Crash... FedEx Flight 80

topics.hook: At 6:49 in the morning, a cargo jet touched down at Narita. It would touch down three times.
cause_chain: A high sink rate approach in strong gusty wind, autothrottle on, airspeed and attitude unstable
A late flare: hard landing and the first bounce
Large nose-down elevator input: the second touchdown on the nose gear, porpoising
The third touchdown: the load from the left main gear overloads the wing structure, the wing breaks, fuel spills and burns
topics.rule_after: JTSB final report adopted 5 April 2013, with safety recommendations to the FAA (26 April 2013) to reduce severe hard landings on the MD-11 and to address gear-to-wing overload under a mainly vertical load.
topics.human_moment: Only the two pilots were aboard the cargo flight.
topics.angle: Why does a wing break on a runway? The fuse pin that should let the gear break away first was designed for a rearward load; on the third touchdown the load was mostly vertical, so it went into the wing.
topics.why_now: The niche's biggest breakout Short in the scan (7.6M on a 27.1K channel, 282x) is this crash; a settled event with a final JTSB report and a clear mechanism no one in the scan explained.

topics.title: Tacoma Narrows, 1940: a new suspension bridge twisted itself apart in a 42 mph wind, four months after it opened

topics.hook: In November 1940, a brand-new bridge in Washington State began to twist in a steady wind. By 11:10 it was gone.
topics.angle: Why did a steady, moderate wind destroy a bridge built for far worse?
